questions.question: Two services each compute SHA-256 over the same 40 million ledger rows and get the same 32-byte digest. What can they conclude?
options: The rows are probably equal, with a small false-positive rate like a Bloom filter
The rows are equal, unless someone has found a SHA-256 collision
The row counts match but the contents might differ in a few bytes
Nothing until they also compare the row count and a checksum
questions.explanation: Collision resistance means equal digests imply equal inputs for any practical purpose; there is no false-positive rate to reason about. A Bloom filter gives probabilistic answers because it discards information; a cryptographic hash of the full input does not.

questions.question: Leaves are hashed as H(0x00 || data) and internal nodes as H(0x01 || left || right). What attack do the prefix bytes prevent?
options: Reordering two adjacent leaves so that the root hash stays the same despite the swap
Appending an extra leaf to the list without changing the root hash at the top
Presenting a fake 64-byte leaf equal to two child hashes so it hashes to a real node
Recovering the original posting bytes from its 32-byte leaf hash by brute force
questions.explanation: Without prefixes, a crafted leaf whose bytes are exactly left||right has the same hash as the internal node above those children, so a forged inclusion proof verifies. The prefixes make leaf and node inputs distinct. Reordering already changes the root because hashNode is order-sensitive; prefixes are not what prevents it.

questions.question: A tree has 5 leaves. Under the carry-up rule, how many sibling hashes are in the inclusion proof for leaf 4 (the last one)?
questions.explanation: Leaf 4 has no partner at level 0, is carried up to level 1 (3 nodes, still unpaired) and to level 2 (2 nodes), where it finally pairs with the hash of leaves 0-3. One sibling. Leaves 0-3 each have three siblings; proofs vary in length under carry-up.

questions.question: Primary and replica each build a tree over the same 8 postings; the replica has one wrong amount at index 5. How many hash comparisons does the pruned diff make?
questions.explanation: One at the root, then two at each of the three levels below, descending only into the half that differs: 1 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 7. A full compare would read all 8 leaves on both sides; 15 is the total number of nodes, which the pruned walk never visits.

questions.question: A verifier holds a trusted root and receives leaf bytes plus a proof that verifies. Which statement is NOT established by the proof?
options: The leaf bytes are present, unmodified, in a tree with that root
Flipping one side tag in the proof would make verification fail
The posting with the next id is absent from the ledger
The proof's length is about log2 of the number of leaves
questions.explanation: An inclusion proof proves presence of one exact leaf; a tree over an unsorted list cannot prove that anything is absent, which needs a sorted or sparse Merkle tree. The other three statements all follow from the construction.

questions.question: Bitcoin pairs an odd last node with a copy of itself. What is the consequence that CVE-2012-2459 exploited?
options: Proofs for the last leaf are longer than for other leaves
The lists [p0..p4] and [p0..p4,p4] produce the same root
The root depends on the order the leaves are hashed
The tree height grows by one level for every odd leaf
questions.explanation: Duplicating the odd node makes a list with a genuinely repeated last element indistinguishable from the odd list, so two different inputs share one root and a cached 'bad block' hash can match a valid block. Carrying the node up avoids this because the leaf counts, and therefore the roots, differ.
